items.title: Number sets and properties
items.content: Natural numbers are counting numbers; whole numbers include zero; integers include negatives. Rational numbers are ratios of integers with nonzero denominator. Use factors, multiples, parity and divisibility to simplify work.

items.title: Estimation and arithmetic
items.content: Estimate first, calculate with place value and operation properties, then check using an inverse operation or bounds.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Estimate before calculating and check after.
Keep units attached through every step.

items.title: Place-value arithmetic and regrouping
items.content: Worked example: \(4,708+2,695=7,403\). Add by place value, regrouping 10 ones as 1 ten, and so on.

items.title: Factors, multiples and divisibility
items.content: Worked example: 468 is divisible by 3 because \(4+6+8=18\), and divisible by 9 for the same reason; it is not divisible by 5.

items.title: Order of operations
items.content: Worked example: \(36/3+4(5-2)=12+12=24\). Brackets first, then division and multiplication, then addition.

items.title: Estimation and bounds
items.content: Worked example: \(198\times51\) is near \(200\times50=10,000\); exact result 10,098 is plausible.

items.title: Integers and sign reasoning
items.content: Worked example: a temperature rises from −6°C by 11°C, reaching \(-6+11=5^\circ\mathrm C\).

items.title: Multi-step word problems
items.content: Translate quantities and units before choosing operations. Worked example: 8 notebooks at ₹35 each and a ₹50 discount cost \(8\cdot35-50=₹230\).

items.title: Mental calculation
items.content: Rewrite around a convenient number. Worked example: \(49\times18=50\times18-18=882\).

items.title: Estimate then calculate
items.content: Round to nearby easy values for a check, then calculate exactly. Worked example: \(602/29\) is near \(600/30=20\); exact quotient is just above 20.

items.title: Divisibility or remainder
items.content: Use a suitable test, then verify. Worked example: remainder of 257 divided by 5 is 2 because \(257=5\cdot51+2\).

items.title: Compare or order numbers
items.content: Align place values or use a common unit; for negatives, the number farther left is smaller. Worked example: −3 < −1 < 0 < 2; on the number line, farther left means smaller.

items.title: Reverse-operation problem
items.content: If a result follows addition/multiplication, undo with subtraction/division and verify in the original statement. Worked example: after adding 7 a number becomes 19, so it was 19 − 7 = 12; check 12 + 7 = 19.

items.title: Why place-value regrouping works
items.content: Ten units of one place equal one unit of the next place because the base is ten: \(10\) ones = \(1\) ten and \(10\) tens = \(1\) hundred.

items.title: Why digit sums test divisibility by 9
items.content: Each power of ten leaves remainder 1 on division by 9, so a number has the same remainder as the sum of its digits.

items.title: Why estimation is a check, not an exact answer
items.content: Rounding changes the inputs slightly. It bounds or approximates the result but does not replace the required exact calculation.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Ignoring units
items.content: Convert quantities to one unit before combining or comparing.

items.title: Accepting an implausible estimate
items.content: Recheck operation choice, decimal placement, and sign if the exact answer is far from the estimate.

items.title: Confusing factor and multiple
items.content: A factor divides a number; a multiple is obtained by multiplying it by an integer.

items.title: Skipping inverse check
items.content: Use addition/subtraction or multiplication/division to verify multi-step results.

keyTakeaways: Place value supports regrouping and decimal arithmetic.
Divisibility tests can reduce lengthy calculations.
Estimation catches many arithmetic and scale errors.

proofsAndDerivations: Why digit sums test divisibility by 9
